newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW--Nippon Mining to seek listing next year.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW--Nippon Mining to seek listing next year.

text.p: Nippon Mining and Metals Co, Japan's largest copper smelter, hopes to raise 15-20 billion yen through a share listing planned for next year.

"We are thinking of placing about 25 million shares, hopefully at a price of around 800 yen each," senior managing director Yasuyuki Shimizu told Reuters, adding the company hoped to raise 15 to 20 billion yen through the listing.
A listing has been planned for Nippon Mining since 1992 when it was spun-off from Japan Energy Corp, which itself was formerly known as Nippon Mining Co Ltd.

Nippon Mining weathered problems arising from the parent company's acquisition of U.S. Gould Inc, which forced Japan Energy to post a group net loss of 16 billion yen in 1996/97, but struggled as a weaker dollar undermined its smelting profits in 1994 and 1995.
"We've got quite heavy borrowings. Our equity to asset ratio stands below 16 percent," Shimizu said.
"Though the listing would not solve the problem immediately, we hope to raise the ratio to about 40 percent, the average among Japanese manufacturers, as soon as possible."
The smelter also needs to raise money to expand into overseas mining as well as for its metal manufacturing business.
"Unless you put money into mines, you can't expect a stable supply of ore," Shimizu said. "We are aiming at integration of smelting and mining."

The company hopes to obtain about two-thirds of its copper ore supply from associated mines -- compared with about 30 percent at the moment -- from late 1999 when the expansion of Chile's Los Pelambres copper mine is due to be completed.

Together with four other Japanese firms, including Mitsubishi Materials Corp, Nippon Mining has signed a contract to take a 40 percent stake in a $1.3 billion project at the Los Pelambres copper mine to boost copper output by 260,000 tonnes per year by September 1999.

This is in addition to Chile's Collahuasi Copper Project, in which Nippon Mining and two other Japanese firms purchased a 12 percent stake in a $1.76 billion project that should yield 750,000 tonnes of copper concentrates a year from 1999.
In its metal manufacturing sector, the company created a new division in April to promote its coating business as well as copper parts which are mainly used in cathode ray tubes.

"In the long term, with only the refining business, we can't expect growth to be as fast as people wish. So we want to expand the metal manufacturing business as has been requested by our customers," Shimizu said.
As part of this effort, Nippon Mining set up a joint venture in Malaysia in December to build a 700 million yen copper parts plant, which should start operations in 1998.
"As far as the Japanese economy is concerned, it might grow a little but we cannot expect a lot, so we are eyeing the Asian market," Shimizu said.

"Unfortunately we have not gone so far as to build smelting facilities abroad. So for a while, we want to sell copper refined in Japan. But it (building a refinery abroad) might become a goal in the long term," he added.
